idiom_name: marker value (usually null or unset) plus a guarded accessor
implementation_notes: Language-neutral structure: keep the value in a cell that can express 'not built yet', and route every read through one accessor that tests the marker, runs the initializer, publishes the result and returns it, so the initializer runs at most once. Under concurrency the guard must be a real once-primitive or an atomic publication step - a plain boolean/null test is neither atomic nor ordered and lets two callers build, or one caller observe a partially built object. Decide the failure policy explicitly: does a failed attempt stay failed, or is it retried on the next access? Where the language binds laziness to syntax or the standard library (function-local statics, once types, lazy bindings, cached properties) that mechanism replaces the hand-written marker test; the classic structure is still justified where the runtime offers nothing, where the initialisation must not be tied to a single variable, or where the cell has to be reset.
pitfalls: A plain check-then-set guard is a race: two callers can run the initializer and a third can observe a published object that is not fully built.
Caching a failed attempt turns a transient error into a permanent one; retrying on every access turns a broken dependency into a latency and log amplification problem - choose deliberately.
Lazy does not mean unmanaged: the built value still needs a lifetime and a release rule (dispose, invalidation, reset) that matches its owner.

Re-entrant initialization deadlocks or panics: an initializer that re-enters the same cell (calls the accessor from inside the build logic) deadlocks with OnceLock, infinitely recurses with most other mechanisms, or throws a mechanism-specific error — keep the initializer narrow and free of callbacks into the owner.

Python's functools.cached_property is not safe for mutable cached data: the cached value is stored as a plain instance attribute, so concurrent mutation from multiple threads can corrupt it even though the initial computation is thread-safe. Use a lock or a different mechanism when the cached value must remain mutable.

Non-volatile double-checked locking (pre-Java-5, pre-C++11, hand-rolled C) publishes a partially constructed object: the guard check races with the write of the reference, and a second thread can see the reference as non-null while the object's fields are still zero-initialized.

Caching a failed initialization attempt permanently: some Lazy<T> forms (LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication in .NET) cache exceptions and rethrow on every subsequent access — a transient failure becomes a permanent failure visible only to callers that hit the accessor.

Lazy initialization of a mutable singleton via a shared mutable cell creates a thread-safe singleton anti-pattern: two threads racing to initialize see different values, breaking the singleton contract. Use the language's once-primitive (std::call_once, sync.Once, std::once_flag) to enforce exactly-once semantics.

Wrong move: Let an Entity Framework Core navigation property trigger lazy database loads inside a loop -> each getter can add a round trip and create an N+1 query -> instead shape the query with explicit or eager loading when the access set is known.

Wrong move: Make mandatory configuration or authorization lazy -> startup can appear successful and fail on an unrelated first accessor -> instead validate required dependencies at the startup or request boundary and reserve laziness for optional work.

Wrong move: Wrap a runtime or framework lazy loader in a second hand-rolled guard -> competing cells obscure publication, exception, and reset semantics -> instead use the owning Lazy<T>, OnceLock, or loader mechanism and configure its documented policy.
